Regarding the statement in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* that "one may not beg three times," this refers to begging three times by making a formal declaration of purity (*jñapti*) at the appropriate price.
21. The Precept on Keeping an Extra Alms Bowl. Regarding why one may keep [an extra bowl] for more than ten days:
it is because the transformation of objects is not constant, and there may be instances of loss or misplacement.
The essential requirements for sustaining the body must not be neglected;
if one does not take them at the time of giving, they will later become difficult to obtain.
For this reason, a ten-day period is established through ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*).
If one keeps them beyond the limit, it constitutes an offense.
The rest is as in the *Dīrghacīvara* rule;
likewise, there is no offense if there are extenuating circumstances such as forgetfulness, as in that case.
The requisites for the body are divided into internal and external:
the alms bowl is an internal requisite, whereas robes are an external necessity. 22.
The Precept on Begging for a Bowl. Regarding the twenty-second precept on begging for a bowl, as explained in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts):
It should be stated as follows:
For example, if Upananda obtained ten sets of bowls by begging from those who were not his relatives,
he should be made to relinquish them.
He seized nine of the alms bowls and brought them into the permanent property of the monastery;
he filled the remaining one with water,
fearing that the monks might examine it closely and thus cause a delay.
The attendant shall cause this to be done among the assembly of monks.
The monk who is begging for the bowl shall hold the bowl and pass it before the senior monk;
the senior monk shall examine it, and if it is good, pour water into the senior monk’s bowl.
The one who has passed [the bowl] shall pass the bowl to that bhikṣu.
Having received it, that bhikṣu shall pass it to the next senior monk in rank.
Having received it, the senior monk shall examine it; if it is superior, [he shall keep it].
He immediately exchanged it for water as before and poured it into [the bowl],
returning it to that bhikṣu who had requested the bowl.
Having received it, he passed it on in this manner from one to another until it reached the end of the assembly.
If the bowls of the middle or lower-ranking monks are of poor quality,
they shall immediately exchange them for those [better] bowls.
This method of practice applies to the seating order of one robe, from the seat of honor down through the subsequent seats.
The entire Saṃgha performed the formal act of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation),
permitting him to carry this single alms-bowl at all times.
The old bowl should also be maintained and used as before;
both must not be separated,
and they must not be intentionally damaged.
If another person or a skillful means breaks a new bowl, there is no offense.
However, if one continues to use an old bowl that has broken, one commits an offense.
If one takes this extra bowl and formally accepts it through the ritual procedure (*dharmakarma*), one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (the forfeiture and confession offense).
He shall repent within the Saṃgha.
Once his offense has been expiated, the Saṃgha shall take back that extra bowl.
If it is of high value, its value shall be sold and the proceeds shall be collected.
Entrust it to a permanent resident of the monastery;
with a small amount of money, purchase a suitable bowl and return it to him for him to maintain.
When walking with the alms bowl, one must proceed within the boundaries of the monastic community. 23.

The precept against begging for thread and having a non-relative weave it (The Twenty-third Precept). 24. The precept against encouraging a weaver regarding thread for a monk’s robe (The Twenty-fourth Precept). 25. The precept against taking back a robe (The Twenty-fifth Precept): Taking it back oneself or causing another to take it back.
Causing another to give and taking it oneself;
causing another to give and having another take it;
giving oneself and taking it oneself.
There are also four permutations:
first, giving separately and seizing collectively; second, giving collectively and seizing separately.
Third, taking together what was given together;
fourth, taking separately what was given separately.
Both cases refer to instances involving multiple robes.
The offense is incurred at the time of taking,
not at the time of giving.
If that person has broken the precepts and lacks dignified deportment, one commits no offense in taking [their property].
If one calculates it, even if the four grave prohibitions (*caturmahāpatti*) are broken, they may be excused.
"Seizing" refers to taking [the property] without concealing it;
if one seizes and removes it without concealment, there is no offense.
26. The Precept Against Possessing Seven-Day Medicine Beyond the Limit. Regarding the twenty-sixth precept against possessing seven-day medicine beyond the limit:
the "first day's medicine" refers to the medicine taken on the initial day.
Regarding the "seven-day medicine," it is the same as the "second-day medicine";
when the dawn of the eighth day appears, it is precisely the end of the seven days.
If it has not been seven days,
this refers to medicinal substances from the third day up to the fifth day;
it is permitted to return them to their original owners for external use, such as for foot ointments or lighting lamps.
Regarding the five things that lack conditions:
there is no loss, seizure, burning, or drifting away as conditions. 27.

The precept against seeking rain-clothing before the [proper] time and using it before the [proper] time. 27. Regarding "obtaining it during the two times": [it refers to obtaining it during the two specific periods].
This refers to the time for seeking robes,
which is from the sixteenth day of the third month onwards.
If one obtains them before the sixteenth day of the third month, [it is not permitted].
This means that once the transgression has been committed, there is no further use for it after seeking [expiation] and completing the rite.
If the sixteenth day of the seventh month has already passed, it is considered "subsequent use.
If one uses it on the sixteenth day of the third month, [it is considered timely].
This exceeds the previous usage.
If one seeks it during the three months of summer or the three months of autumn,
it should be worn by the sixteenth day of the seventh month.
It should not be used in one place;
if it is used there, it will bring good fortune.
Furthermore, it need not be discarded.
It is to be used as usual the following year.
The *Liao lun* states:
"As for the rain-cloak (*varṣāśāṭī*), it is necessary because one must protect the three robes."
If, while traveling on a road, one perceives that it is about to rain, one should take this robe and cover the body with it.
When traveling on a road during heavy rain,
one should remove the three robes, hang them against a wall or post, and travel wearing this robe.
One may also wear this robe while bathing in the rain or in an open space.
The term "bathing" (yù) is used here in its general sense of being moistened;
it does not mean that one is wearing the robe specifically for the purpose of bathing.
The *śāṭī* is the same as the *antarvāsaka*.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"On the sixteenth day of the third month, one should seek [the material] and prepare [the robe]; this applies likewise until the fifteenth day of the fourth month."
From the sixteenth day of the third month until the end of the month, one may seek to have robes made.
If the robes are completed, they may be kept from the first day of the fourth month, but it is not permitted to use them.

If the robes are not completed by the fifteenth day of the fourth month, it is permitted to continue seeking them or having them made; however, regarding the date, it is as previously stated: on the first day of the fourth month, they may only be kept and not used.
Because it is used on the same day as the commencement of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*),
this differs from the *Caturvargika-vinaya*,
which stipulates that bathing should be performed every half-month.
It may be used starting from the first day of the fourth month.
If it is discarded for other uses, or if it is worn for bathing, washed, or set aside,
these are all permitted as exceptions to the rules regarding its loss.
The full text states:
"The group of six bhikṣus, at all times—whether summer or winter—constantly sought rain-cloths and did not relinquish them;
they then used the rain-cloths for other purposes."
Seeing that people were still bathing naked despite the existence of rain-cloths,
[the Buddha] even rebuked them, saying:
"One should not act in this manner."
The subsequent explanatory text states:

"Regarding those who have committed an offense, they may seek [the robe] on the sixteenth day of the third month for use on the first day of the fourth month; this is the aforementioned allowance for a *pāyattika* offense. However, once the rain-cloth has been relinquished, it may not be used for any other purpose."
If one bathes while wearing a bathing robe and does not bathe naked;
if there is no rain-cloak or if one makes a rain-cloak;
if it is washed or dyed; or if the place where it is kept is deep—there is no offense.
The ten kinds of robes are:
first, cotton robes;
second, white linen robes.
Third, garments made of wool;
fourth, garments made of stored hemp;
fifth, garments made of wild hemp.
Sixth, garments of hemp;
seventh, garments of white sheep’s wool;
eighth, garments of bird feathers.
9. *Jiāng* (vermilion) is also correct;
it refers to clothing made of wool in the color *jiāng*.
10. *Páng* (variegated) refers to clothing made of wool in a variegated color.
Regarding the rain-bathing robe, it was because of Viśākha.
Whenever he invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha,
his maidservant would announce that the time had come when she saw [the preparations].
The bhikṣus bathed naked in the rain and consequently made eight vows.
After inviting the Buddha to a meal, they took a low seat and sat before the Buddha.
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me this wish.
The Buddha said, "As you desire."
He said:
"A guest bhikṣu has arrived from afar;
we do not know his destination or his wishes."
"World-Honored One, please listen to me.
I wish to provide food for visiting bhikṣus for as long as I live.
There are two bhikṣus traveling from afar."
Or, thinking it was for the sake of food, he did not accompany his companion;
let me permit him to travel afar,
and that the bhikṣu shall provide for him with food for as long as he lives.
A bhikṣu who was ill with a chronic disease was unable to eat as he pleased and consequently passed away.
Fourth, if you permit me to eat according to my illness, that illness may be cured;
fourth, provide medicinal substances as desired to the sick bhikṣu;
fifth, provide food to the bhikṣu who attends to the sick.
Sixth, he constantly listened to the bhikṣus' recitation of the *poṣadha*.
Seventh, he gave rain-cloths to the bhikṣus.
Eighth, he gave bathing robes to the bhikṣuṇīs.
28. The Precept on Urgently Offered Robes. This twenty-eighth precept on urgently offered robes is also known as "not being permitted to keep them beyond the earlier limit or after the later limit.
Once the sixth day of the seventh month has passed, it is permitted to receive [the robe]; receiving it before that time is not allowed.
Regarding "urgent robe-gift" (*ātyayikakāṭhina*):
it is called an urgent robe-gift because it is given due to an urgent cause or circumstance.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there are five types of urgent robe-gifts.
If an army intends to march urgently,
it is a "past-time" gift;
it is not a "subsequent" gift.
The *Ji shi er yao jing* (Twelve Essentials of the Jetavana) states:
Regarding "urgent robes," it refers to when a man or a woman living at home is about to undergo a rite of tonsure.
When returning from a military expedition,
at the time of death,
and when women return home.
If a donor says to a bhikṣu,
"If you do not take it today, there will be none tomorrow," this is called an urgent gift.
Having already gone to listen and receive [the teachings] on the sixth day of the seventh month,
there remain ten days in total until the sixteenth; during this time,
one may receive urgent offerings.
Regarding those without a cause or condition:
if there is loss, seizure, or any of the four such conditions, one is permitted to keep the robe beyond the prescribed time limit.
If a monk who has entrusted his robe travels far away, and the water route is cut off or interrupted, he may keep it after the period has elapsed.
Because these two offenses cannot be committed simultaneously under this precept:
if one has already committed the prior offense, one does not subsequently commit the later one.
Third, "within ten days" means:
If one obtains a robe more than ten days after [the designated period],
such as obtaining it on the fifth day of the seventh month, it is called an offense; however,
if it was received before that time had elapsed, there is no offense.
Because it is defined as "keeping" [the robe], it must be kept within ten days.
That is to say, if one obtains it on the sixteenth day of the seventh month, since one has not yet committed an offense prior to that time, it is pure;
only after the designated period has passed does one commit the offense of keeping it beyond the limit.
This is because the robe does not constitute a repeated offense.
For instance, if one receives an urgent offering robe on the fourteenth day of the seventh month,
it may be kept for two days.
One immediately enters the month of Kārttika.
Outside of Kārttika, eight days are still open.
Thus, having received [the precepts] on the thirteenth day, one may subsequently receive them for seven days or twelve days.
One should receive [the precepts] on the seventh day of the month;
thereafter, for the remaining days prior to that,
one may open [the items] on the very next day.

29. The Precept on Separating from One’s Robes in a Forest Hermitage during Times of Distress. Regarding the twenty-ninth precept on separating from one’s robes in a forest hermitage during times of distress, there are five circumstances that constitute "no cause":
namely, when there are dangers such as those to life or to the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya).
It is not a violation if one does not combine robes when permitted by specific circumstances.
To clarify those with many conditions:
first, there are bhikṣus who observe the rainy season retreat in an araṇya (forest hermitage).
If one goes out for alms and the room is opened by a wood-gatherer or a cowherd carrying a door-hook, who then steals the clothing and takes it away,
one may listen to [the rule on] entrusting clothing because there is fear of losing the garment.
This very thing serves as the condition;
there is no fixed time limit.
As for the two conditions:
Because Upāli had discarded his purified robes,
he feared that if it rained again he would be unable to bear the weight;
the Buddha therefore permitted him to be separated from his robes.
Question: When will he return?
Ānanda calculated that he would stay two days after departing and two days before returning, totaling six days.
For this reason, six days were opened;
this is the second circumstance.
As for "there must be other circumstances":
Furthermore, this case of Upāli going to and fro with the Saṃgha and being granted a period of six nights is one instance of external circumstances.
As for the transgression arising from the monks of a village:
At that time, when the followers of the fourfold division were storing robes without setting a time limit,
a fire broke out in a village;
the forest-dwelling bhikṣus feared the fire would burn their robes.
The assembly at night regarding robes and bedding gave rise to an occasion for censure;
consequently, the rule of six nights was established, though the specific circumstances were not made explicit.
Thus, those who today stubbornly cling to their own views are mistaken.
The ancient masters said:
"If there is doubt or fear, one may only open [the period] for six nights;
if it exceeds that, one incurs an offense."
Since the fixed six-night penance was established because [the offense] arose due to transgression,
why would it be further permitted in the text only for conditions such as fear, while other conditions are not permitted?
The ancient masters maintained that this applies solely when there is a condition of fear.
To permit [the practice] only once is a false attachment.
Now, according to the various schools, it is permitted whenever there is a valid cause.
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, regarding the *stūpa*, the *upādhyāya*, and other such cases,
all permit the six-night period.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā*) permits it at all times when the hearing of the Dharma has not yet been completed.
In the text of the *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra*, multiple conditions are not clarified,
nor is it stated that there are many [conditions].
Since "condition" (*pratyaya*) does not manifest the specific characteristics of the conditions, [the text remains silent on this point].
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* does not further mention circumstances such as the presence of a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), a teacher (*ācārya*), or matters concerning stupas (*stūpa*).
Since these points are not stated in the text that permits [the practice],
it is said that the characteristics of the specific conditions are not made explicit.
Regarding the statement that "the rest is as explained in the rules for those living in the same village," this refers to the opening passage of this very precept:
"If one abandons the assembly, loses [the robe], is robbed, or faces terror and peril."
As with the preceding precepts, I shall not cite them at length;
therefore, they are summarized here.
Regarding the entrusting of robes within a village:
The six nights, the assembly, the acts of losing, seizing, burning, and so forth, are inseparable.

30. The precept against diverting the property of the Sangha into one's own possession. Regarding the thirtieth precept on diverting the property of the Sangha into one's own possession, there are two distinctions between that which has not yet been distributed and that which belongs to individual members of the Sangha.
This is because it is definitively granted to that *saṃgha*, without making a distinction between "this" and "that.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, if a donor offers property for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony to one *saṃgha* and redirects it to another, [it constitutes an offense].
Question: If this were definitively attached [to the object], then one would commit a *pārājika* offense as soon as the object is returned;
if it is not definitively attached, then upon the completion of the act, one commits a *duṣkṛta*.
Why is it said that one must first become a Non-returner (Anāgāmin) for the offense to be considered grave?
Thus we know that the various schools differ;
the underlying intent has not yet been fully understood.
